newsitem.title: JAPAN: NTT half-year profits surge on Internet use.
newsitem.headline: NTT half-year profits surge on Internet use.

text.p: Japanese telecommunications giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp reported sharply higher half-year profits on Friday, aided by strong revenues from Internet and cellular phone users.
The 63.9 percent jump in interim profits at NTT's parent company beat market expectations, and NTT and analysts said the results point to a positive future.
"New demand is growing in new service areas and we see that as a bright sign on the horizon," NTT president Junichiro Miyazu told a news conference.

Eric Gan, analyst at Goldman Sachs (Japan) Corp, said: "It was the first time that NTT managed to raise its profits without boosting phone rates. It showed that NTT can boost its profits without a company split-up," he said.
The results boosted NTT's share prices on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, closing up 41,000 yen ($369) at 820,000 yen ($7,387) on Friday.

A heavy cloud hanging over NTT was also expected to be cleared soon as both the government and the company made it clear on Friday that they hope to reach a decision as early as December on whether to break up the company.

NTT said its parent current profit -- which is before tax and includes extraordinary items -- shot up to a recent half-year high of 207.75 billion yen ($1.87 billion), up 63.9 percent over a year earlier.
The gain came despite large rate cuts on domestic long-distance calls and leased lines, which cut into NTT's half-year profits by 47 billion yen ($423 million).

A cellular phone boom and soaring demand for communications via computers boosted NTT's phone traffic, pushing up its revenues from the telephone business by 35.3 billion yen ($318 million) to 1.32 trillion yen ($11.8 billion), NTT said.
This includes interconnection charges from booming cellular phone operators, which were 44 billion yen ($396 million) more than a year earlier, NTT said.

The charges, for connecting competitors fragmented networks into NTT's local-call network, grew nearly 70 percent to around 300 billion yen ($2.7 billion) in total, when those paid from long-distance operators are included, NTT said.
NTT, which is still 65 percent owned by the government, monopolises Japan's local-call networks.
Consumers eager to access the Internet and other on-line services also flocked to NTT's digital communications lines, called integrated circuit for digital networks (ISDN).
Revenues from ISDN, which allows sending and receiving data about three times as fast as over ordinary phone lines, more than quadrupled to 99 billion yen ($891 million).
ISDN, provided almost solely by NTT in Japan, uses regular telephone lines but needs digital network terminals on both ends of the line.
NTT expects to gain 800,000 new ISDN customers in the current business year, exceeding the approximately 600,000 new ordinary analogue phone customers it expects.
Revenues from high-speed digital leased lines and construction of local-area networks also contributed, NTT said.
NTT also managed to cut its personnel costs by 36.4 billion yen ($327 million) as a result of a reduction in staff of 4,700 to 186,000. ($1=111 yen)
